tier_reason: The ugrep-indexer README shows exact commands and timings: cold unindexed ugrep 1.02s, ripgrep 13.0.0 1.18s, indexed ugrep 0.0487s (best of 4, range 0.0487-0.0983s, '21 times faster' vs unindexed). These are first-party numbers with no CPU, OS or compiler stated, so tier C.

corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the project's own README (ugrep-indexer) with exact commands shown, but no CPU model, OS, or compiler flags are stated, and the dataset is small (1,317 files, 12.2MB, old ugrep v3.12.6 tree; ripgrep 13.0.0). The '21x' figure compares indexed vs ugrep's own unindexed run; the ~12x-24x vs-ripgrep figure is derived from page data. The two tools were timed differently: ugrep through its internal --stats timer, ripgrep through shell `time` wall clock (which includes process startup). The ugrep-indexer repo's last commit is 2025-06-22.

notes: Claim and derived ratios check out (1.18/0.0487 = 24.2x, 1.18/0.0983 = 12.0x). ugrep has 3,302 stars, BSD-3-Clause, not a fork. Its default branch (master) last commit is 2026-09-15; the 2026-09-21 push was a dependabot branch.

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md compares directly against Go stdlib unicode/utf8 using public code (bench_parity_test.go, BenchmarkParity*). It states Apple M4 Max, Go 1.26.4, `-benchtime=0.3s -count=3` and gives the exact reproduce command, which meets tier A. The amd64 section runs on a GitHub Actions EPYC runner (GOAMD64=v1, Go 'stable', -count=6). The README adds an IBM z15 run (go1.26.4, -count=6).

corrections.claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md, Apple M4 Max NEON: Valid ASCII 1.21x-2.21x; Valid multibyte-mixed 1.90x-9.0x (1 MiB: 3.87 vs 0.43 GB/s); RuneCount 3.58x-8.7x vs unicode/utf8. amd64 AVX2 GitHub Actions EPYC runner: Valid ASCII 2.06x-3.65x, Valid mixed 3.66x-19.74x (1 MiB: 5196 vs 263 MB/s), RuneCount 4.81x-21.08x. Separately, the README reports Valid 19.07x on EPYC 7763 (5940 vs 312 MB/s, ~1 MiB mixed buffer) and IBM z15 s390x results of 1.96x (ASCII 16 KiB), 1.73x (ASCII 1 MiB), 10.4x (mixed 1 MiB) and 9.5x (RuneCount 1 MiB). The README's ~4.6x RuneCount figure came from a QEMU-hosted x86 VM, not native hardware.
corrections.workload: Valid (UTF-8 validation, Lemire-Keiser lookup algorithm) and RuneCount on printable-ASCII and multibyte-mixed (a/e-acute/lambda/CJK/emoji) buffers, 64 B-1 MiB, single core, BenchmarkParity* harness vs unicode/utf8. Run on Apple M4 Max NEON and a GitHub Actions AMD EPYC AVX2 runner (BENCHMARKS.md); IBM z15 s390x results are in the README.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.4 (M4 Max arm64 and z15 runs); Go 'stable' via setup-go on the amd64 CI runner; GOAMD64=v1 on amd64; go test -bench=Parity -benchtime=0.3s -count=3 (arm64), -count=6 (amd64, s390x)
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Max (arm64 NEON, macOS); GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest AMD EPYC runner (7763 or 9V74 depending on run, AVX2, no AVX-512); IBM z15 (s390x, VXE2, real hardware, 2026-07-03, per README)
corrections.caveats: Very new, low-usage project (0 stars), so treat this as an early-stage result. The amd64 numbers come from a shared GitHub Actions runner whose EPYC part varies between runs: absolute MB/s is noisy, but same-job ratios are valid. The pure-ASCII path regressed 5-8x vs stdlib on amd64, and ran at 0.13x on s390x, until a recent ASCII pre-scan fix; the arm64 NEON kernel was only added on 2026-06-22. The README's 4.6x RuneCount figure was measured under QEMU. ppc64le figures are llvm-mca estimates, not measurements.

notes: The record's specific numbers (19.07x, 5940/312 MB/s, z15 ratios, 4.6x) are in README.md#performance, not in the cited BENCHMARKS.md. BENCHMARKS.md has newer and generally larger ratios (up to 21x on amd64, up to 9x on an M4 Max), so I rewrote claimed_speedup from it rather than downgrading. Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-08, not a fork.

tier_reason: Tier upgraded to A on stronger evidence. The repo README's x64 results name an Intel Xeon Gold 6548N and .NET 10 (AVX-512), and the public BenchmarkDotNet code (benchmark/Benchmark.cs, net10.0, run with `dotnet run -c Release`) benchmarks against a vendored copy of the runtime's Utf8Utility.GetPointerToFirstInvalidByte. The cited blog post alone is first-party with only a microarchitecture name ('Ice Lake'), which would be C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (.NET 10, AVX-512): up to 14x on Emoji-Lipsum (15 vs 1.1 GB/s), 2.5x on Twitter.json (36 vs 14 GB/s), 2.8x-9.1x on other non-ASCII lipsum sets, and slower than .NET on pure-ASCII Latin-Lipsum (72 vs 107 GB/s). Apple M2: 1.5x-4.1x (Twitter.json 1.8x, 25 vs 14 GB/s). Graviton 3 / Neoverse V1 / Qualcomm 8cx gen3 / Graviton 2: 1.2x-5.8x. The earlier blog post (2024-06-20) reported Ice Lake up to 13x on emoji and 2.4x on Twitter.json (29 vs 12 GB/s).
corrections.baseline: .NET runtime's built-in UTF-8 validator (Utf8Utility.GetPointerToFirstInvalidByte; private in the runtime, benchmarked through a vendored MIT copy in benchmark/UTF8_runtime.cs)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET 10 (net10.0), BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.4, `dotnet run -c Release`; AVX-512 kernel on x64, NEON on ARM; .NET version not stated for the ARM tables
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (x64 AVX-512); Apple M2; AWS Graviton 3 (Neoverse V1); Qualcomm 8cx gen3; Graviton 2 (Neoverse N1). Earlier blog run: Intel Ice Lake
corrections.workload: UTF-8 validation (GetPointerToFirstInvalidByte) of Twitter.json and lipsum texts in Arabic, Chinese, emoji, Hebrew, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Latin and Russian, with BenchmarkDotNet on x64 (AVX-512) and several ARM64 systems
corrections.stars_or_usage: 49 stars; the author (Lemire) proposed it for the .NET runtime in dotnet/runtime issue #103781 (open)
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (simdutf/Lemire team). The baseline is a vendored copy of the runtime's private validator compiled into the benchmark, not the shipped BCL call path. On pure ASCII (Latin-Lipsum), .NET 10's own validator is faster on x64 (107 vs 72 GB/s). .NET version is not stated for the ARM results. Low adoption (49 stars).

notes: The blog numbers in the record are accurate. The README has newer, fully specified x64 results (Xeon Gold 6548N, .NET 10), so I moved benchmark_url there and upgraded the tier to A. Issue #103781 was opened by lemire himself, so 'flagged as a candidate' is a self-proposal. Metadata matches: MIT, 49 stars, last commit 2026-08-19.

tier_reason: The README tables (NEON armv8a and SSE4 E5-2650) are the original author's own numbers, not peer-reviewed or independent. The benchmark code (main.c, './utf8 bench') is public and gcc-7.3 is named, but no optimization flags or ARM CPU model are stated, so this is first-party with partial methodology: C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: NEON (armv8a): range2 1579.85 MB/s vs Lemire 1198.50 MB/s on UTF-8-demo.txt (~1.32x, derived from page data). On synthetic buffers range2 beats Lemire by ~1.17x (32 B: 1043.58 vs 891.38) up to ~1.78x (33 B: 1048.12 vs 588.77), and ~1.32x at 1K-1M (derived from page data). SSE4 (Xeon E5-2650): range2 is at parity with Lemire (3986.13 vs 3954.74 MB/s on demo text; 3960.49 vs 3923.51 at 1M) and slower at 32 B (2173.02 vs 2890.52). Vs naive byte-by-byte validation on demo text: ~2.8x on NEON (1579.85 vs 562.25) and ~5.3x on SSE4 (3986.13 vs 753.70) (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-7.3 (stated in the protobuf-bundled README: 'Built and tested with gcc-7.3'); optimization flags not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: Bundled into Google Protocol Buffers (72k stars) as third_party/utf8_range; ScyllaDB's utils/utf8.cc uses the range algorithm and credits cyb70289/utf8. Originally developed in cyb70289/utf8 (85 stars, MIT) and the now-archived protocolbuffers/utf8_range (21 stars)
corrections.caveats: First-party README benchmark with no optimization flags and no ARM CPU model (only 'armv8a'). The tables benchmark the original research files (range-neon.c, range2-*.c, lemire-*.c); protobuf's shipped utf8_range.c is a 2023 Google wrapper (ASCII fast path, then range-sse), which these numbers do not cover. The baseline is Lemire's 2018 fastvalidate-utf-8 prototype, not current simdutf. On x86 SSE4 the gain over Lemire is within noise and reversed at 32 B, so the win is ARM-specific. The component is MIT-licensed; protobuf as a whole is BSD-3-Clause.

notes: The numbers match the page, but the '~20-32% consistent edge' was wrong: the NEON edge over Lemire ranges from 17% to 78% by size. Last commit touching third_party/utf8_range is 2026-06-19 (kept); the protobuf repo's overall last commit is 2026-09-25. The component LICENSE file is MIT (Yibo Cai 2019 and Google 2022), not BSD-3-Clause.

tier_reason: The author's 2016 blog has ratio tables vs ICU 55 (Ubuntu 16.04 build): English UTF-8 decode 7.23 and encode 7.00, other-language UTF-8 decode 1.64-3.92, UTF-16LE/BE 0.30-0.32. The benchmark code is public (hsivonen/encoding_bench), but no CPU model (only 'Haswell') or compiler version/flags are given, so tier C.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (author's own blog, Nov 2016) against ICU 55, a decade-old ICU release built by Ubuntu's toolchain that may not reflect current ICU. The author notes ICU's build flags and compiler may differ from ICU as used in browsers. Only the microarchitecture (Haswell) is given, with no CPU model or rustc version/flags. The benchmark harness is hsivonen/encoding_bench. Some directions (UTF-16LE/BE) are slower than ICU. The Cargo license is '(Apache-2.0 OR MIT) AND BSD-3-Clause'; the BSD-3-Clause part covers WHATWG-derived data.

notes: All claimed ratios are on the page (English 7.23/7.00; non-English UTF-8 decode 1.64-3.92; UTF-16 0.30-0.32). The GitHub spdx is NOASSERTION; Cargo.toml plus the LICENSE-APACHE, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-WHATWG files give the corrected expression. 467 stars, last commit 2026-09-24, not a fork, not archived.
